notes.front: What did “self-organizing” mean in Scrum Guides before 2020?
notes.back: Development Teams choosing who does the work and how.
notes.explanation: The 2020 Guide put the emphasis on a self-managing Scrum Team instead, with more focus on the Scrum Team as a whole.
notes.example: Like a band that decides who plays which part and how, while someone else still picks the set list; self-management adds choosing what to play.
notes.source: Scrum Guide Revision History, “Changes between 2017 and 2020 Scrum Guides”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What was the “Development Team” in Scrum Guides before 2020?
notes.back: The team of people within the Scrum Team who did the work of creating the Increment.
notes.explanation: The 2020 Guide removed this separate team within a team; there is now one Scrum Team, and the people doing the work are Developers.
notes.example: Like a squad inside a club with its own boundary; since 2020 there is only the club, and “Developers” names an accountability, not a squad.
notes.source: Scrum Guide Revision History, “Changes between 2010 and 2011 Scrum Guides”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the Scrum Guide require of the Developers regarding the Definition of Done?
notes.back: That they conform to it.
notes.explanation: The wording is “required”, so conformance is not something the Developers can set aside under pressure.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”
notes.evidence: The Developers are required to conform to the Definition of Done.

notes.front: Who structures and empowers Scrum Teams to manage their own work?
notes.back: The organisation.
notes.explanation: Self-management depends on the organisation around the team, not only on the team’s own wish to manage itself.
notes.evidence: They are structured and empowered by the organization to manage their own work. Working in Sprints at a sustainable pace improves the Scrum Team’s focus and consistency.

notes.front: What does working in Sprints at a sustainable pace improve, according to the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: The Scrum Team’s focus and consistency.
notes.explanation: The Guide places this straight after saying the organisation structures and empowers Scrum Teams to manage their own work.
notes.evidence: They are structured and empowered by the organization to manage their own work. Working in Sprints at a sustainable pace improves the Scrum Team’s focus and consistency.

notes.front: What have the Scrum Guide’s authors found about smaller teams, in general?
notes.back: They communicate better and are more productive.
notes.explanation: The finding is hedged with “in general”, and the Guide gives team size as typically 10 or fewer people.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team is small enough to remain nimble and large enough to complete significant work within a Sprint, typically 10 or fewer people. In general, we have found that smaller teams communicate better and are more productive.

notes.front: What may the Developers choose for their Daily Scrum, and on what two conditions?
notes.back: Any structure and techniques, as long as it focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal and produces an actionable plan for the next day.
notes.explanation: The Guide says this freedom creates focus and improves self-management.
notes.evidence: The Developers can select whatever structure and techniques they want, as long as their Daily Scrum focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal and produces an actionable plan for the next day of work. This creates focus and improves self-management.

notes.front: Daily Scrums improve {{c1::communications}}, identify impediments, promote quick decision-making, and consequently eliminate the need for other meetings.
notes.explanation: Communication heads the Guide’s list of four benefits; the last, fewer other meetings, follows from the others.
notes.evidence: Daily Scrums improve communications, identify impediments, promote quick decision-making, and consequently eliminate the need for other meetings.

notes.front: Daily Scrums improve communications, {{c1::identify impediments}}, promote quick decision-making, and consequently eliminate the need for other meetings.
notes.explanation: Impediments found each day feed the Scrum Master’s work of causing their removal.
notes.evidence: Daily Scrums improve communications, identify impediments, promote quick decision-making, and consequently eliminate the need for other meetings.

notes.front: Daily Scrums improve communications, identify impediments, {{c1::promote quick decision-making}}, and consequently eliminate the need for other meetings.
notes.explanation: Quick decisions suit the event’s purpose of adapting the Sprint Backlog as necessary.
notes.evidence: Daily Scrums improve communications, identify impediments, promote quick decision-making, and consequently eliminate the need for other meetings.

notes.front: Daily Scrums improve communications, identify impediments, promote quick decision-making, and consequently {{c1::eliminate the need for other meetings}}.
notes.explanation: The Guide says “consequently”: this benefit follows from the other three.
notes.evidence: Daily Scrums improve communications, identify impediments, promote quick decision-making, and consequently eliminate the need for other meetings.

notes.front: What did the 2020 Scrum Guide do with the Daily Scrum questions?
notes.back: It removed them.
notes.explanation: The revision history lists this among changes meant to make the Guide less prescriptive and return Scrum to a minimally sufficient framework.
notes.source: Scrum Guide Revision History, “Changes between 2017 and 2020 Scrum Guides”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the 2017 Scrum Guide, were the three Daily Scrum questions mandatory?
notes.back: No. They were an example; the Development Team set the structure, and some teams used discussion instead.
notes.explanation: Even then the event could be run in different ways, as long as it focused on progress toward the Sprint Goal.
notes.source: Scrum Guide Revision History, “Changes between 2016 and 2017 Scrum Guides”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the Scrum Guide describe the Sprint Backlog during the Sprint?
notes.back: A highly visible, real-time picture of the Developers’ planned work, updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.
notes.explanation: The Guide says “consequently”: because it is a real-time picture, it changes as learning happens.
notes.evidence: It is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work that the Developers plan to accomplish during the Sprint in order to achieve the Sprint Goal. Consequently, the Sprint Backlog is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.

notes.front: How much detail should the Sprint Backlog have, according to the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: Enough for the Developers to inspect their progress in the Daily Scrum.
notes.explanation: This links the artifact to the event: the Daily Scrum inspects progress, so the plan must be detailed enough to show it.
notes.evidence: It should have enough detail that they can inspect their progress in the Daily Scrum.

notes.front: What behaviour did the 2020 Scrum Guide aim to end by removing the separate team within a team?
notes.back: The Product Owner and the Development Team acting as two opposing sides, or dealing with each other through go-betweens.
notes.explanation: There is now one Scrum Team focused on the same objective, with three different sets of accountabilities.
notes.source: Scrum Guide Revision History, “Changes between 2017 and 2020 Scrum Guides”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does self-managing (2020 Guide) differ from self-organizing (earlier Guides)?
notes.back: Self-organizing Development Teams chose who and how; the self-managing Scrum Team chooses who, how and what to work on.
notes.explanation: The change also moved the emphasis from the Development Team to the whole Scrum Team.
notes.source: Scrum Guide Revision History, “Changes between 2017 and 2020 Scrum Guides”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between the old “Development Team” and today’s “Developers”?
notes.back: The Development Team was a separate team within the team; Developers is one of three sets of accountabilities in one Scrum Team.
notes.explanation: The other two sets of accountabilities are the Product Owner’s and the Scrum Master’s.
notes.source: Scrum Guide Revision History, “Changes between 2017 and 2020 Scrum Guides”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The Product Owner insists that the Developers use a particular database design she read about. The Developers think it is wrong for the product. What should the Scrum Master do?
notes.back: C: help the Product Owner see that how to build it is the Developers’ decision.
notes.choices:
A) Back the Product Owner, as she is accountable for value
B) Split the difference by using her design for half the items
C) Help the Product Owner understand that how to build the Increment is the Developers’ decision, while she can share needs and constraints
D) Ask a manager to choose between the two designs
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Product Owner’s accountability for value does not extend to how the work is done. B: the decision still belongs to the Developers, not to a compromise imposed from outside. D: no one else tells the Developers how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments.
notes.explanation: The Guide puts the “how” at the sole discretion of the Developers.
notes.evidence: How this is done is at the sole discretion of the Developers. No one else tells them how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments of value.

notes.front: An architect from another department joins Sprint Planning and starts assigning technical tasks to individual Developers. What should the Scrum Master do?
notes.back: C: help the architect see that the Developers plan the work, and welcome the advice as input.
notes.choices:
A) Let it continue, as the architect has more experience
B) Ask the architect to leave Sprint Planning at once
C) Help the architect understand that the Developers plan how to do the work, and that their advice is welcome as input
D) Take over the assigning so it stays inside the Scrum Team
notes.choicesExplained: A: experience does not change who decides: no one else tells the Developers how. B: the Scrum Team may invite others to Sprint Planning to give advice; the problem is the assigning, not the presence. D: the Scrum Master assigning tasks is no better than the architect doing it.
notes.explanation: The Guide lets the team invite others to give advice at Sprint Planning, while how the work gets done stays with the Developers.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team may also invite other people to attend Sprint Planning to provide advice.

notes.front: The Scrum Master, a former engineer, is sure the Developers’ planned design will cause trouble later. What fits the Scrum Guide best?
notes.back: D: share the concern as input and leave the decision to the Developers.
notes.choices:
A) Ask the Product Owner to make the design a requirement
B) Insist on the better design, since the Scrum Master is accountable for effectiveness
C) Say nothing, since design is none of the Scrum Master’s business
D) Offer the concern as input, leaving the decision with the Developers
notes.choicesExplained: B: effectiveness comes from enabling the team, not from directing how it works. C: sharing a view is not telling the Developers how; staying silent withholds useful input. A: this uses the Product Owner to tell the Developers how, which no one else does.
notes.explanation: The Developers decide how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments, whoever else has a view.
notes.evidence: How this is done is at the sole discretion of the Developers. No one else tells them how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments of value.

notes.front: One Developer keeps skipping the code reviews the team agreed on. The others complain privately to the Scrum Master. What is the best first step?
notes.back: D: coach the Developers to raise it with him directly.
notes.choices:
A) Speak to him on the team’s behalf so that nobody feels awkward
B) Report the matter to his line manager
C) Remove code reviews from the working agreement
D) Coach the Developers to raise it with him directly, holding each other accountable as professionals
notes.choicesExplained: A: this takes over an accountability the Guide gives to the Developers. B: this adds a hierarchy the Scrum Team does not have. C: dropping the practice avoids the conversation rather than dealing with it.
notes.explanation: Holding each other accountable as professionals is one of the things the Guide says Developers are always accountable for.
notes.evidence: Holding each other accountable as professionals.

notes.front: A line manager asks the Scrum Master which Developer is “carrying the team” and which is not. What is the most helpful response?
notes.back: D: the Developers hold each other accountable, and the whole Scrum Team is accountable for the Increment.
notes.choices:
A) Refuse to discuss the team with the manager at all
B) Give a frank ranking, as the manager has a right to know
C) Ask the Developers to rate each other anonymously for the manager
D) Explain that the Developers hold each other accountable as professionals and the whole Scrum Team is accountable for the Increment
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide gives accountability to the team as a whole and to the Developers among themselves. C: this turns peer accountability into reporting upward. A: the Scrum Master serves the organisation by helping it understand Scrum.
notes.explanation: The Guide makes the entire Scrum Team accountable for a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint.
notes.evidence: The entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint.

notes.front: A director tells the Developers to skip the automated regression tests in their Definition of Done, to hit a trade-show date. What should the Scrum Master help everyone see?
notes.back: A: the Definition of Done is required; renegotiate scope with the Product Owner instead.
notes.choices:
A) The Developers are required to conform to the Definition of Done; the date is better met by renegotiating scope with the Product Owner
B) The director can waive the Definition of Done for one release
C) The Developers may skip tests if they fix any defects next Sprint
D) The Scrum Master should decide which tests to skip
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide requires conformance, and no one outside the team can waive it. C: quality does not decrease during the Sprint. D: the Scrum Master has no authority to lower the Definition of Done either.
notes.explanation: Scope, not quality, is what the Guide lets the team renegotiate with the Product Owner.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”
notes.evidence: The Developers are required to conform to the Definition of Done.

notes.front: The Definition of Done requires user documentation. The Developers propose counting an item as finished now and writing its documentation next Sprint. What happens to the item under the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: D: it is not Done, so it is not in the Increment and returns to the Product Backlog.
notes.choices:
A) It counts as Done, with the documentation as a follow-up item
B) It may be released, but not shown at the Sprint Review
C) The Product Owner may accept it as Done on her own authority
D) It does not meet the Definition of Done, so it is not part of the Increment and returns to the Product Backlog
notes.choicesExplained: A: an item is Done only when it meets the Definition of Done. B: an item that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be released either. C: the Developers are required to conform to the Definition of Done; the Product Owner cannot waive it.
notes.explanation: The Guide says an item that does not meet the Definition of Done returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”
notes.evidence: If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. Instead, it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.

notes.front: Midway through the Sprint, the Sprint Goal looks at risk. A Developer suggests lowering the team’s test coverage for the rest of the Sprint. What should the Scrum Master remind the team?
notes.back: C: quality does not decrease; renegotiate scope with the Product Owner instead.
notes.choices:
A) Lowering coverage is fine if the Sprint Goal is met
B) The Sprint should be extended until the goal is safe
C) Quality does not decrease during the Sprint; scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner instead
D) The Sprint Goal should be replaced with an easier one
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide lists “quality does not decrease” among the rules for the whole Sprint. B: Sprints are fixed-length events. D: no changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal; renegotiating scope is the tool.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s rules for the Sprint protect quality and the Sprint Goal, and leave scope open to renegotiation.
notes.evidence: During the Sprint: - No changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal; - Quality does not decrease; - The Product Backlog is refined as needed; and, - Scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned.

notes.front: By the second week, the Developers see that the work for the Sprint Goal is larger than they expected. Which response fits the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: B: work with the Product Owner to renegotiate Sprint Backlog scope, keeping the Sprint Goal.
notes.choices:
A) Work nights and weekends to complete the full forecast
B) Collaborate with the Product Owner to negotiate the scope of the Sprint Backlog without affecting the Sprint Goal
C) Relax the Definition of Done for this Sprint only
D) Quietly drop items without telling anyone
notes.choicesExplained: A: sustained overtime works against the sustainable pace that improves focus and consistency. C: quality does not decrease during the Sprint. D: scope is renegotiated with the Product Owner, openly.
notes.explanation: The Guide expects work to turn out differently at times, and gives the Developers and Product Owner a way to adjust scope while keeping the goal.
notes.evidence: If the work turns out to be different than they expected, they collaborate with the Product Owner to negotiate the scope of the Sprint Backlog within the Sprint without affecting the Sprint Goal.

notes.front: The Developers must wait weeks for a manager’s approval before changing any tool they use, even a free one. What should the Scrum Master work toward?
notes.back: C: an organisation that empowers the team to manage its own work.
notes.choices:
A) A faster approval form, so requests take days instead of weeks
B) The Scrum Master approving tools instead of the manager
C) An organisation that structures and empowers the team to manage its own work, including such choices
D) A rule that the team never changes tools during a Sprint
notes.choicesExplained: A: a quicker gate still keeps the decision away from the team managing its work. B: this replaces one approver with another. D: this adds a restriction instead of empowering the team.
notes.explanation: The Guide says Scrum Teams are structured and empowered by the organisation to manage their own work, so the change needed is in the organisation.
notes.evidence: They are structured and empowered by the organization to manage their own work. Working in Sprints at a sustainable pace improves the Scrum Team’s focus and consistency.

notes.front: For months, the team has worked weekends to meet each Sprint forecast, and a manager praises its “commitment”. What should the Scrum Master raise with the team?
notes.back: C: a sustainable pace improves focus and consistency; forecasts can use past performance and capacity.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: the team is showing the value of commitment
B) That the Sprints should be longer so the weekends are not needed
C) That working at a sustainable pace improves focus and consistency, and that forecasts can draw on past performance and capacity
D) That the Scrum Master will set lower forecasts from now on
notes.choicesExplained: A: commitment in Scrum is to goals and each other, not to unsustainable hours. B: lengthening Sprints does not fix forecasting, and it reduces learning cycles. D: the Developers make the forecast; the Scrum Master helps them improve it.
notes.explanation: The Guide ties a sustainable pace to focus and consistency, and says the more the Developers know about past performance and capacity, the more confident their forecasts.
notes.evidence: They are structured and empowered by the organization to manage their own work. Working in Sprints at a sustainable pace improves the Scrum Team’s focus and consistency.

notes.front: A Scrum Team of fourteen finds that its Daily Scrum always overruns and many people feel out of touch. What should the Scrum Master raise?
notes.back: C: team size, since smaller teams generally communicate better.
notes.choices:
A) Extending the Daily Scrum to 30 minutes
B) Holding separate Daily Scrums for front-end and back-end specialists within the one team
C) The team’s size as a likely factor, since in general smaller teams communicate better and are more productive
D) Banning discussion at the Daily Scrum
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event. B: within a Scrum Team there are no sub-teams. D: the Developers choose its structure; the problem lies in communication across a large group.
notes.explanation: The Guide describes Scrum Teams as typically 10 or fewer people and links smaller size to better communication.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team is small enough to remain nimble and large enough to complete significant work within a Sprint, typically 10 or fewer people. In general, we have found that smaller teams communicate better and are more productive.

notes.front: At each Daily Scrum, the Developers take turns reporting to the Scrum Master what they did yesterday. No one changes the plan, even when the Sprint Goal is at risk. What should the Scrum Master help them do?
notes.back: C: refocus it on progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapting the Sprint Backlog.
notes.choices:
A) Report in more detail, so the Scrum Master can plan for them
B) Add a second daily meeting for re-planning
C) Refocus the event on inspecting progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapting the Sprint Backlog
D) Stop meeting, since status can be read from the board
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Sprint Backlog is the Developers’ plan, not the Scrum Master’s. B: the Daily Scrum itself is where the plan is adapted. D: the event exists to inspect and adapt, not to report status.
notes.explanation: The Guide defines the Daily Scrum’s purpose as inspecting progress toward the Sprint Goal and adjusting the upcoming work.
notes.evidence: The purpose of the Daily Scrum is to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog as necessary, adjusting the upcoming planned work.

notes.front: The Product Owner, who works on no Sprint Backlog items, attends every Daily Scrum and hands out tasks. The Developers have stopped planning for themselves. What should the Scrum Master do?
notes.back: D: help the Product Owner see it is the Developers’ event, and coach the Developers to plan.
notes.choices:
A) Run the Daily Scrum personally so that neither side dominates
B) Let it continue, as the Product Owner knows the priorities best
C) Ban the Product Owner from ever speaking to the Developers
D) Help the Product Owner see that the Daily Scrum is the Developers’ event, and coach the Developers to plan their own day
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Daily Scrum is for the Developers; the Product Owner orders the Product Backlog, not the day’s tasks. C: collaboration with the Product Owner is expected; the problem is the assigning. A: this still takes the event away from the Developers.
notes.explanation: The Guide makes the Daily Scrum an event for the Developers, joined by the Product Owner as a Developer only when working on Sprint Backlog items.
notes.evidence: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers of the Scrum Team. To reduce complexity, it is held at the same time and place every working day of the Sprint. If the Product Owner or Scrum Master are actively working on items in the Sprint Backlog, they participate as Developers.

notes.front: Several stakeholders want to attend the Daily Scrum each morning “to keep up with progress”. What should the Scrum Master suggest?
notes.back: B: it is the Developers’ event; stakeholders can use the Sprint Backlog and the Sprint Review.
notes.choices:
A) Let them attend and ask questions, to build trust
B) Explain that the Daily Scrum is an event for the Developers, and point stakeholders to the visible Sprint Backlog and to the Sprint Review
C) Send them a daily written summary from the Scrum Master
D) Hold a second daily meeting just for stakeholders
notes.choicesExplained: A: turning the event into a briefing for others takes it away from the Developers’ planning. D: Daily Scrums are meant to reduce the need for other meetings, not add them. C: this adds reporting instead of using the transparency the artifacts already give.
notes.explanation: The Sprint Backlog is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work, and the Sprint Review is where stakeholders inspect the outcome.
notes.evidence: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers of the Scrum Team. To reduce complexity, it is held at the same time and place every working day of the Sprint. If the Product Owner or Scrum Master are actively working on items in the Sprint Backlog, they participate as Developers.

notes.front: A new team member insists that every Daily Scrum must follow three fixed questions, “as Scrum requires”. What is accurate?
notes.back: A: the questions were removed; the Developers choose any structure meeting the two conditions.
notes.choices:
A) The 2020 Guide removed the questions; the Developers may use any structure that focuses on the Sprint Goal and produces a plan for the next day
B) The three questions are still required by the Scrum Guide
C) The questions are required, but only for new teams
D) The Scrum Master decides which questions the team uses
notes.choicesExplained: B: the revision history records that the 2020 Guide removed them. C: the Guide sets no rule for new teams; the structure is the Developers’ choice. D: the Developers select the structure and techniques.
notes.explanation: The structure belongs to the Developers, bounded only by the focus on the Sprint Goal and a plan for the next day.
notes.evidence: The Developers can select whatever structure and techniques they want, as long as their Daily Scrum focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal and produces an actionable plan for the next day of work. This creates focus and improves self-management.

notes.front: The Developers run their Daily Scrum by walking the board item by item, from nearest-to-done to newest. A manager objects: “That isn’t a proper Daily Scrum.” Who is right?
notes.back: A: the Developers, if it focuses on the Sprint Goal and yields a plan for the next day.
notes.choices:
A) The Developers, as long as it focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal and produces an actionable plan for the next day
B) The manager: the Scrum Master must approve any structure
C) The manager: each person must give an individual update
D) Neither: the Daily Scrum must follow the Product Owner’s agenda
notes.choicesExplained: C: the Guide prescribes no person-by-person format. B: the Developers select the structure and techniques themselves. D: the Daily Scrum is an event for the Developers, not the Product Owner.
notes.explanation: The Guide says choosing their own structure creates focus and improves self-management.
notes.evidence: The Developers can select whatever structure and techniques they want, as long as their Daily Scrum focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal and produces an actionable plan for the next day of work. This creates focus and improves self-management.

notes.front: Besides the Daily Scrum, the Developers hold a daily status call, a technical sync and a blockers meeting. What should the Scrum Master help them inspect?
notes.back: A: whether their Daily Scrum works as intended, since a good one removes the need for other meetings.
notes.choices:
A) Whether their Daily Scrum is working as intended, since a good one improves communication, surfaces impediments and speeds decisions, removing the need for other meetings
B) Nothing, since more communication is always better
C) Merging all three into one longer meeting after the Daily Scrum
D) Cancelling the Daily Scrum, since the other meetings cover it
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide says Daily Scrums should eliminate the need for other meetings. C: this keeps an extra meeting instead of asking why the Daily Scrum is not enough. D: the Daily Scrum is a Scrum event; dropping it loses its purpose.
notes.explanation: Extra meetings doing the Daily Scrum’s job suggest the event is not delivering its benefits.
notes.evidence: Daily Scrums improve communications, identify impediments, promote quick decision-making, and consequently eliminate the need for other meetings.

notes.front: The Developers save their blockers for the Sprint Retrospective, so some go unaddressed for two weeks. What should the Scrum Master help them see?
notes.back: C: the Daily Scrum is meant to surface impediments every day.
notes.choices:
A) Blockers belong in the Sprint Retrospective, so the team is right
B) Blockers should be emailed to the Scrum Master only
C) The Daily Scrum is meant to identify impediments, so blockers can surface and be acted on every day
D) Blockers should wait for the Sprint Review with stakeholders
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide lists identifying impediments among the Daily Scrum’s benefits. B: this keeps them from the Developers, who plan around them. D: waiting delays an adjustment that should be made as soon as possible.
notes.explanation: Identifying impediments is one of the four things the Guide says Daily Scrums improve.
notes.evidence: Daily Scrums improve communications, identify impediments, promote quick decision-making, and consequently eliminate the need for other meetings.

notes.front: At 11:00, two Developers discover a problem that changes the plan for the rest of the Sprint. One says: “Let’s bring it to tomorrow’s Daily Scrum.” What should the Scrum Master encourage?
notes.back: D: adjust the plan now; the Daily Scrum is not the only time to do it.
notes.choices:
A) Waiting for the Daily Scrum, as that is when the plan changes
B) Raising it at the Sprint Retrospective
C) Asking the Scrum Master to re-plan the Sprint
D) Adapting the plan now: the Daily Scrum is not the only time the Developers may adjust it
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide says Developers often meet throughout the day to re-plan. B: the Sprint Retrospective comes at the end of the Sprint, and the plan needs adjusting now. C: the Sprint Backlog is the Developers’ plan.
notes.explanation: The Guide expects Developers to meet during the day for detailed discussions about re-planning.
notes.evidence: The Daily Scrum is not the only time Developers are allowed to adjust their plan. They often meet throughout the day for more detailed discussions about adapting or re-planning the rest of the Sprint’s work.

notes.front: Which of these statements about the Daily Scrum matches the 2020 Scrum Guide?
notes.back: C: a 15-minute event for the Developers, in their chosen structure, focused on the Sprint Goal.
notes.choices:
A) It is a 15-minute event for the Development Team, answering three set questions
B) It is a meeting where the Scrum Master collects status for the Product Owner
C) It is a 15-minute event for the Developers, in whatever structure they choose, focused on the Sprint Goal
D) It is optional when the team sits together
notes.choicesExplained: A: this mixes pre-2020 wording: the Development Team is gone, and the questions were removed. B: the Guide gives it to the Developers to inspect progress and adapt their plan. D: it is held every working day of the Sprint.
notes.explanation: The 2020 changes removed both the Development Team and the questions, leaving the structure to the Developers.
notes.evidence: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers of the Scrum Team. To reduce complexity, it is held at the same time and place every working day of the Sprint. If the Product Owner or Scrum Master are actively working on items in the Sprint Backlog, they participate as Developers.

notes.front: The team’s Sprint Backlog is updated once a week, by the Scrum Master, from notes. What should change?
notes.back: A: the Developers keep it up to date in real time as they learn.
notes.choices:
A) The Developers should keep it as a real-time picture, updated throughout the Sprint as they learn
B) Nothing, as long as the updates are accurate
C) The Product Owner should update it daily instead
D) It should be frozen after Sprint Planning to protect the plan
notes.choicesExplained: B: a weekly snapshot is not the real-time picture the Guide describes. C: the Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers. D: the Guide says it is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.
notes.explanation: A plan that lags a week cannot support inspection at the Daily Scrum.
notes.evidence: It is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work that the Developers plan to accomplish during the Sprint in order to achieve the Sprint Goal. Consequently, the Sprint Backlog is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.

notes.front: A manager sees the Developers add and split tasks in the Sprint Backlog mid-Sprint and calls it “scope creep”. How should the Scrum Master respond?
notes.back: D: the Sprint Backlog changes as more is learned; the Sprint Goal is what stays protected.
notes.choices:
A) Agree and freeze the Sprint Backlog
B) Tell the manager that the Sprint Backlog is secret
C) Ask the Developers to make changes only at the Sprint Review
D) Explain that the Sprint Backlog is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned; what stays protected is the Sprint Goal
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide expects it to change throughout the Sprint. C: the Sprint Review inspects the outcome; the plan changes during the Sprint. B: it is meant to be highly visible.
notes.explanation: The Guide builds flexibility into the plan while protecting the Sprint Goal from changes that would endanger it.
notes.evidence: It is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work that the Developers plan to accomplish during the Sprint in order to achieve the Sprint Goal. Consequently, the Sprint Backlog is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.

notes.front: At Sprint Planning, the Developers announce that they will spend the whole Sprint refactoring instead of the Product Owner’s top items: “We’re self-managing, so we decide what to work on.” What should the Scrum Master help them see?
notes.back: D: self-management works within the accountabilities; items are selected with the Product Owner.
notes.choices:
A) They are right: self-managing means they choose their work alone
B) They are wrong: only the Product Owner decides what the Developers do
C) The Scrum Master should split the Sprint half and half
D) Self-management works within Scrum’s accountabilities: the Developers select items through discussion with the Product Owner, who orders the Product Backlog
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide has the Developers select items through discussion with the Product Owner. B: the Developers do select items for the Sprint, with the Product Owner, not by order. C: the decision belongs to the Scrum Team, not to the Scrum Master.
notes.explanation: The 2020 Guide adds “what” to self-management, but in Sprint Planning the choice is made with the Product Owner.
notes.evidence: Through discussion with the Product Owner, the Developers select items from the Product Backlog to include in the current Sprint.

notes.front: A trainer says: “The team chooses who does the work and how; someone else decides what they work on.” Which Scrum Guide wording does this match?
notes.back: C: The pre-2020 self-organizing wording
notes.choices:
A) The Nexus Guide’s wording
B) The 2020 self-managing wording
C) The pre-2020 self-organizing wording
D) The Definition of Done
notes.choicesExplained: B: self-managing adds “what” to “who and how”. A: this description comes from the Scrum Guide’s own history. D: the Definition of Done describes the Increment’s quality, not who decides what.
notes.explanation: The revision history contrasts self-organizing (who and how) with self-managing (who, how and what).
notes.source: Scrum Guide Revision History, “Changes between 2017 and 2020 Scrum Guides”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The Product Owner and the Developers talk only through a business analyst, and each side blames the other when things go wrong. What should the Scrum Master work toward?
notes.back: D: one Scrum Team with the Product Owner and Developers collaborating directly.
notes.choices:
A) A formal hand-off document between the two sides
B) Making the business analyst the Product Owner’s official proxy
C) Separate Sprint Reviews for the Product Owner and the Developers
D) One Scrum Team working toward the same objective, with the Product Owner and Developers collaborating directly
notes.choicesExplained: A: this entrenches the us-and-them split the 2020 Guide set out to end. B: proxy behaviour is exactly what the one-team change aimed to remove. C: there is one Scrum Team, not two sides.
notes.explanation: The 2020 Guide removed the team within a team to end proxy and us-and-them behaviour between the Product Owner and the people doing the work.
notes.source: Scrum Guide Revision History, “Changes between 2017 and 2020 Scrum Guides”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The Developers call themselves “the dev team” and say the Sprint Goal is “the Product Owner’s problem”. What should the Scrum Master help them understand?
notes.back: B: there is one Scrum Team, and the whole team defines the Sprint Goal.
notes.choices:
A) They are right: the Product Owner owns the Sprint Goal alone
B) There is one Scrum Team, and the whole Scrum Team collaborates to define the Sprint Goal
C) The Sprint Goal is optional if the Product Backlog is ordered
D) The Scrum Master owns the Sprint Goal
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide says the whole Scrum Team collaborates to define it. D: no single person owns it; the whole Scrum Team defines it. C: the Sprint Goal must be finalised before the end of Sprint Planning.
notes.explanation: The Product Owner proposes how the product could increase its value, and the whole Scrum Team then defines the goal.
notes.evidence: The whole Scrum Team then collaborates to define a Sprint Goal that communicates why the Sprint is valuable to stakeholders. The Sprint Goal must be finalized prior to the end of Sprint Planning.

notes.front: The Developers ask the Scrum Master to write their Sprint Backlog plan, because they are “too busy coding”. What is the best response?
notes.back: C: coach them to create their own plan.
notes.choices:
A) Write it, since it frees up time for delivery
B) Ask the Product Owner to write it
C) Coach them to create the plan themselves, as it is their accountability
D) Skip the plan and let everyone pick work as they go
notes.choicesExplained: A: creating the Sprint Backlog is an accountability the Guide gives the Developers. B: the plan is by and for the Developers, not the Product Owner. D: the Sprint Backlog must be detailed enough to inspect progress at the Daily Scrum.
notes.explanation: A plan written by someone else is not the Developers’ plan, and planning is how they self-manage.
notes.evidence: However, the Developers are always accountable for: - Creating a plan for the Sprint, the Sprint Backlog;

notes.front: The front-end specialists in a Scrum Team want to form their own sub-team with its own board and planning. What should the Scrum Master help them understand?
notes.back: B: there are no sub-teams within a Scrum Team.
notes.choices:
A) Sub-teams are fine if they share the same Product Owner
B) Within a Scrum Team there are no sub-teams; the team works as one cohesive unit toward one objective
C) Sub-teams are fine if they keep a joint Daily Scrum
D) The Scrum Master should lead the new sub-team
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide says there are no sub-teams within a Scrum Team. C: the joint event does not undo the split within the team. D: the problem is the split itself, whoever leads it.
notes.explanation: The Guide describes a Scrum Team as a cohesive unit of professionals with no sub-teams or hierarchies.
notes.evidence: Within a Scrum Team, there are no sub-teams or hierarchies.

notes.front: Management appoints a “lead developer” to tell the other Developers what to work on each day. What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: D: no hierarchies; the team itself decides who does what, when and how.
notes.choices:
A) A lead is fine as long as the lead is also a Developer
B) A lead is required once a team has more than five Developers
C) A lead is fine if the Scrum Master approves
D) Within a Scrum Team there are no hierarchies; the team internally decides who does what, when and how
notes.choicesExplained: A: a Developer directing the others is still a hierarchy within the team. B: the Guide sets no such rule. C: the Scrum Master cannot approve a hierarchy the Guide rules out.
notes.explanation: The Guide defines self-managing as the team deciding internally who does what, when and how.
notes.evidence: Within a Scrum Team, there are no sub-teams or hierarchies. It is a cohesive unit of professionals focused on one objective at a time, the Product Goal. Scrum Teams are cross-functional, meaning the members have all the skills necessary to create value each Sprint. They are also self-managing, meaning they internally decide who does what, when, and how.

notes.front: The organisation has a Definition of Done as a standard for all products. One Scrum Team wants to use a lighter version for its internal tool. What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: B: the organisational Definition of Done is the minimum.
notes.choices:
A) The team may use a lighter one for internal products
B) The team must follow the organisational Definition of Done as a minimum
C) The Product Owner may approve a lighter one
D) The team may use a lighter one if the Scrum Master agrees
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide makes the organisational standard a minimum for all Scrum Teams. C: the Guide gives no one that exception. D: the Scrum Master cannot waive an organisational standard.
notes.explanation: The Guide says that where the Definition of Done is an organisational standard, all Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”
notes.evidence: If the Definition of Done for an increment is part of the standards of the organization, all Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum.

notes.front: A Developer who joined yesterday asks the Scrum Master: “Who will tell me what to work on?” What is the best answer?
notes.back: A: the Developers decide together who does what, and she takes part.
notes.choices:
A) The Developers decide together who does what, and she joins in that planning, for example at the Daily Scrum
B) The Scrum Master will assign her work each day
C) The Product Owner will give her a list
D) A senior Developer will be her manager for the first month
notes.choicesExplained: B: the self-managing team decides who does what. C: the Product Owner orders the Product Backlog; the Developers plan the Sprint’s work. D: there are no hierarchies within a Scrum Team.
notes.explanation: Self-managing means the Scrum Team internally decides who does what, when and how.
notes.evidence: They are also self-managing, meaning they internally decide who does what, when, and how.
